newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour claims victory in economic ideas battle.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour claims victory in economic ideas battle.

text.p: Party has won the battle of economic ideas and for the first time in a generation will relish fighting the coming election on the economy, party leader Tony Blair said on Wednesday.

In a pre-election pep-talk to the men and women who would form his cabinet if Labour wins power, aides reported Blair as saying economics spokesman Gordon Brown had cemented the party's new reputation for economic prudence and competence.

The record of the ruling Conservatives, by contrast, had been destroyed by what Blair called a lethal combination of sterling's expulsion from the European exchange rate mechanism in 1992, a doubling of the national debt and 22 tax rises.

Officials said Blair would carry the same message to a breakfast meeting on Thursday with 50 top business executives at which he will commit Labour to publishing a business maanifesto in addition to its main election programme.
"Labour is winning the argument of economic competence with business just as it is winning it with households up and down the land," Blair is expected to tell the businessmen.
He will argue that the Conservatives, in power since 1979, had failed in the three areas of crucial importance to business -- the need for stability, leadership and fiscal prudence.
"For the first time in a generation, it is Labour that is shaping and winning the economic argument," he will say.
Labour leads the Conservatives by 20 percentage points according to a Reuter/NOP poll released this week, but Blair told his "shadow" cabinet to guard against complacency.
He urged his colleagues in the run-up to the election, widely expected to be on May 1, to hammer home the fact that one in five non-pensioner households in Britain has no one in a job.
Labour should also warn that the growth of an underclass was not only a social evil but could also turn into an economic nightmare, Blair said.
The election battle lines were now clear and -- again for the first time in years -- they were of Labour's choosing.

Blair said the choice between a Labour party that looked to the future, represented the many and offered leadership and a Conservative party that looked to the past, stood for the few and was hopelessly adrift.

Officials said Labour leaders were working on the assumption that Prime Minister John Major would delay the election until May -- the last legal date is May 22 -- in the hope that economic recovery would translate into brighter poll ratings.
But Blair argued at the shadow cabinet meeting that delay would in fact damage the Conservatives by reinforcing the impression that it had little to offer, aides said.
